source: Two male rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) were used in the study (O and P).

claim: The monkeys weighed on average 6–7 kg during the experiments.
source: They weighed on average 6–7 kg during the experiments.
evidence: Directly stated measurement of the subjects' weight.

claim: All procedures followed the protocol approved by the Animal Care Committee of Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CEBSIT-2021004).
source: All procedures followed the protocol approved by the Animal Care Committee of Shanghai Institutes for Biological Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CEBSIT-2021004).

claim: The monkeys completed on average 33 ± 9 games in each session.
source: On average, the animals completed 33 ± 9 (mean ± standard error [SE]) games in each session and each game took them 4.9 ± 1.8 attempts (Appendix 1—figure 2).
evidence: Quantitative measurement of game performance reported with statistical measures.

claim: Each game took the monkeys on average 4.9 ± 1.8 attempts.
source: On average, the animals completed 33 ± 9 (mean ± standard error [SE]) games in each session and each game took them 4.9 ± 1.8 attempts (Appendix 1—figure 2).

claim: The monkeys tended to choose the direction with the largest local reward.
source: The monkeys tended to choose the direction with the largest local reward (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and C).

claim: The probability of choosing the most rewarding direction decreased with the growing number of available directions.
source: The probability of choosing the most rewarding direction decreased with the growing number of available directions, suggesting a negative effect of option numbers on the decision-making optimality.
evidence: Behavioral pattern observed in the data with interpretation.

claim: The monkeys tended to avoid the ghosts in the normal mode.
source: As expected, the monkeys tended to avoid the ghosts in the normal mode and chase them when they were scared.
evidence: Behavioral observation reported in the results.

claim: The monkeys chased ghosts when they were scared.
source: As expected, the monkeys tended to avoid the ghosts in the normal mode and chase them when they were scared.
evidence: Behavioral observation reported in the results.

claim: Both monkeys were more likely to run away from Blinky.
source: Accordingly, both monkeys were more likely to run away from Blinky but ignored or even followed Clyde when it was close by.
evidence: Behavioral observation showing differential responses to different ghosts.

claim: Both monkeys ignored or even followed Clyde when it was close by.
source: Accordingly, both monkeys were more likely to run away from Blinky but ignored or even followed Clyde when it was close by.
evidence: Behavioral observation showing differential responses to different ghosts.

claim: Blinky aggressively chases Pac-Man by design.
source: By design, Blinky aggressively chases Pac-Man, but Clyde avoids Pac-Man when they get close (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: Description of the game design and ghost behavior algorithms.

claim: Clyde avoids Pac-Man when they get close by design.
source: By design, Blinky aggressively chases Pac-Man, but Clyde avoids Pac-Man when they get close (see Materials and methods for details).
evidence: Description of the game design and ghost behavior algorithms.

claim: The ghosts were treated the same by the monkeys when in scared mode.
source: On the other hand, the ghosts were treated the same by the monkeys when in scared mode.
evidence: Behavioral observation of monkey responses to scared ghosts.

claim: The monkeys went after the scared ghosts when they were near Pac-Man.
source: The monkeys went after the scared ghosts when they were near Pac-Man.
evidence: Behavioral observation reported in the results.

claim: The dynamic compositional strategy model explains the monkeys' behavior with over 90% accuracy.
source: The model reveals that the monkeys adopted the take-the-best heuristic by using one dominating strategy for their decision-making at a time and formed compound strategies by assembling the basis strategies to handle particular game situations. With the model, the computationally complex but fully quantifiable Pac-Man behavior paradigm provides a new approach to understanding animals' advanced cognition.
evidence: Model performance reported in the abstract.

claim: The model's prediction accuracy is 0.907 ± 0.008 for Monkey O.
source: Overall, the dynamic compositional strategy model explains the monkeys' behavior well. The model's prediction accuracy is 0.907 ± 0.008 for Monkey O and 0.900 ± 0.009 for Monkey P.
evidence: Quantitative model performance metric reported with statistical measure.

claim: The model's prediction accuracy is 0.900 ± 0.009 for Monkey P.
source: Overall, the dynamic compositional strategy model explains the monkeys' behavior well. The model's prediction accuracy is 0.907 ± 0.008 for Monkey O and 0.900 ± 0.009 for Monkey P.
evidence: Quantitative model performance metric reported with statistical measure.

claim: The static strategy model achieves an overall accuracy of 0.806 ± 0.014 for Monkey O.
source: In comparison, a static strategy model, which uses the fixed strategy weights, achieves an overall accuracy of 0.806 ± 0.014 and 0.825 ± 0.012 for monkeys O and P, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of model performance.

claim: The static strategy model achieves an overall accuracy of 0.825 ± 0.012 for Monkey P.
source: In comparison, a static strategy model, which uses the fixed strategy weights, achieves an overall accuracy of 0.806 ± 0.014 and 0.825 ± 0.012 for monkeys O and P, respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of model performance.

claim: During the early game, the local strategy dominated all other strategies.
source: During the early game, defined as when there were more than 90% remaining pellets in the maze, the local strategy dominated all other strategies.
evidence: Analysis of strategy usage in specific game contexts.

claim: During the late game, both the local and the global strategies had large weights.
source: In comparison, during the late game, defined as when there were fewer than 10% remaining pellets, both the local and the global strategies had large weights.
evidence: Analysis of strategy usage in specific game contexts.

claim: The approach strategy came online when one or both scared ghosts were within 10 tiles around Pac-Man.
source: The approach strategy came online when one or both scared ghosts were within 10 tiles around Pac-Man.
evidence: Analysis of strategy usage in specific game contexts.

claim: The most dominating strategy's weights (0.907 ± 0.117) were significantly larger than those of the secondary strategy (0.273 ± 0.233).
source: The histograms of the three dominating strategies' weights from all time points show that the most dominating strategy's weights (0.907 ± 0.117) were significantly larger than those of the secondary strategy (0.273 ± 0.233) and tertiary strategy (0.087 ± 0.137) by a significant margin (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of strategy weights with statistical measures.

claim: The most dominating strategy's weights (0.907 ± 0.117) were significantly larger than those of the tertiary strategy (0.087 ± 0.137).
source: The histograms of the three dominating strategies' weights from all time points show that the most dominating strategy's weights (0.907 ± 0.117) were significantly larger than those of the secondary strategy (0.273 ± 0.233) and tertiary strategy (0.087 ± 0.137) by a significant margin (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of strategy weights with statistical measures.

claim: The monkeys adopted a take-the-best (TTB) heuristic by using a dominant strategy.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that the monkeys adopted a TTB heuristics in which action decisions were formed with a single strategy heuristically and dynamically chosen.
evidence: Interpretation of the strategy weight analysis results.

claim: The monkeys looked at the ghosts more often under the energizer strategy than under the local strategy (p<0.001).
source: Interestingly, the monkeys also looked at the ghosts more often under the energizer strategy than under the local strategy (p<0.001, two-sample t-test), which suggests that the monkeys were also keeping track of the ghosts when going for the energizer.
evidence: Eye tracking data analysis with statistical significance testing.

claim: The pupil diameter exhibited a significant but transient increase around strategy transitions (p<0.01).
source: When averaged across all types of transitions, the pupil diameter exhibited a significant but transient increase around strategy transitions (p<0.01, two-sample t-test, Figure 3F, also individual monkeys: Figure 3—figure supplement 2B–F).
evidence: Pupil dilation analysis with statistical significance testing.

claim: The pupil diameter increase was absent when the strategy transition went through a vague period.
source: Such an increase was absent when the strategy transition went through a vague period.
evidence: Comparison of pupil dilation patterns in different transition types.

claim: The monkeys chose the shortest path when adopting the global strategy.
source: In addition, during the global strategy, the monkeys often moved Pac-Man to reach a patch of pellets far away from its current location. They chose the shortest path (Figure 3C, individual monkeys: Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and G) and made the fewest turns to do so (Figure 3D, individual monkeys: Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and H), demonstrating their goal-directed path-planning behavior under the particular strategy.
evidence: Analysis of trajectory planning behavior with supporting figures.

claim: The monkeys made the fewest turns when adopting the global strategy.
source: In addition, during the global strategy, the monkeys often moved Pac-Man to reach a patch of pellets far away from its current location. They chose the shortest path (Figure 3C, individual monkeys: Figure 3—figure supplement 1C and G) and made the fewest turns to do so (Figure 3D, individual monkeys: Figure 3—figure supplement 1D and H), demonstrating their goal-directed path-planning behavior under the particular strategy.
evidence: Analysis of trajectory planning behavior with supporting figures.

claim: The dataset includes 3217 games, 15,772 rounds, and 899,381 joystick movements.
source: The dataset includes 3217 games, 15,772 rounds, and 899,381 joystick movements.
evidence: Quantitative description of the dataset size.

claim: Each pellet is worth two drops of juice.
source: In the recording sessions, there are 88 or 73 pellets in the maze, each worth two drops of juice, and three or four energizers, each worth four drops of juice.

claim: Each energizer is worth four drops of juice.
source: In the recording sessions, there are 88 or 73 pellets in the maze, each worth two drops of juice, and three or four energizers, each worth four drops of juice.
evidence: Reward structure specification in the task design.

claim: The scared state lasts 14 s.
source: The scared state lasts 14 s, and the ghosts flash as a warning during the last 2 s of the scared mode.
evidence: Game mechanics specification.

claim: The ghosts flash as a warning during the last 2 s of the scared mode.
source: The scared state lasts 14 s, and the ghosts flash as a warning during the last 2 s of the scared mode.
evidence: Game mechanics specification.

claim: Monkeys get eight drops of juice if they eat a ghost.
source: Monkeys get eight drops of juice if they eat a ghost.
evidence: Reward structure specification in the task design.

claim: The average distance between Pac-Man, the energizer, and the ghosts was significantly smaller in planned attack than in accidental consumption (p<0.001).
source: Indeed, the average of distance between Pac-Man, the energizer, and the ghosts was significantly smaller in planned attack than in accidental consumption (Figure 5B, p<0.001, two-sample t-test, individual monkeys: Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–F).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical significance testing.

claim: The monkeys fixated on the ghosts, the energizers, and Pac-Man more frequently before the energizer consumption in planned attacks than in accidental consumption (p<0.001).
source: The monkeys fixated on the ghosts, the energizers, and Pac-Man more frequently before the energizer consumption in planned attacks than in accidental consumption (Figure 5C, p<0.001, two-sample t-test, individual monkeys: Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–G), reflecting more active planning under the way.
evidence: Eye tracking analysis with statistical significance testing.

claim: The monkeys' pupil sizes were smaller before they caught a ghost in planned attacks than in accidental consumption (p<0.01).
source: In addition, the monkeys' pupil sizes were smaller before they caught a ghost in planned attacks than in accidental consumption (p<0.01, two-sample t-test), which may reflect a lack of surprise under planned attacks (Figure 5D, individual monkeys: Figure 5—figure supplement 1D–H).
evidence: Pupil dilation analysis with statistical significance testing and interpretation.

claim: The distance between Pac-Man and the ghosts was greater in suicides than in failed evasions (p<0.001).
source: In addition, the distance between Pac-Man and the ghosts was greater in suicides (Figure 6B, p<0.001, two-sample t-test, individual monkeys: Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and F).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical significance testing.

claim: The monkeys tended to saccade toward the ghosts and pellets more often in suicides than in failed evasions (p<0.001).
source: Consistent with the idea, the monkeys tended to saccade toward the ghosts and pellets more often in suicides than in failed evasions (Figure 6C, p<0.001, two-sample t-test, individual monkeys: Figure 6—figure supplement 1C and G).
evidence: Eye movement analysis with statistical significance testing.

claim: The monkeys' pupil size decreased even before Pac-Man's death in suicides, which was significantly smaller than in failed evasions (p<0.01).
source: Their pupil size decreased even before Pac-Man's death in suicides, which was significantly smaller than in failed evasions, suggesting that the death was anticipated (Figure 6D, p<0.01, two-sample t-test, individual monkeys: Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and H).
evidence: Pupil dilation analysis with statistical significance testing and interpretation.

claim: The ability to use heuristic strategies demands an advanced level of intelligence and has not been demonstrated in animals.
source: The ability to use heuristic strategies demands an advanced level of intelligence and has not been demonstrated in animals.
evidence: Statement about the novelty of the findings in the abstract.

claim: Many have shown that animals exhibit complex strategy-like behaviors.
source: Many have shown that animals exhibit complex strategy-like behaviors (Beran et al., 2015; Bird and Emery, 2009; Brotcorne et al., 2017; Gruber et al., 2019; Leca et al., 2021; Loukola et al., 2017; Reinhold et al., 2019; Sabbatini et al., 2014; Sanz et al., 2010), but quantitative studies are lacking.
evidence: Literature review with multiple citations.

claim: Quantitative studies of complex strategy-like behaviors in animals are lacking.
source: Many have shown that animals exhibit complex strategy-like behaviors (Beran et al., 2015; Bird and Emery, 2009; Brotcorne et al., 2017; Gruber et al., 2019; Leca et al., 2021; Loukola et al., 2017; Reinhold et al., 2019; Sabbatini et al., 2014; Sanz et al., 2010), but quantitative studies are lacking.
evidence: Statement about the gap in the literature.

claim: The level of complexity of the existing animal behavioral paradigms is insufficient for studying how animals manage strategies to simplify a sophisticated task.
source: Moreover, despite the continuing effort in studying complex behavior in animals and the underlying neural mechanisms (Haroush and Williams, 2015; Kira et al., 2015; Ong et al., 2021; Yoo et al., 2020), the level of complexity of the existing animal behavioral paradigms is insufficient for studying how animals manage strategies to simplify a sophisticated task.
evidence: Critical assessment of existing research with citations.

claim: The game is essentially a foraging task for the monkeys.
source: The game was essentially a foraging task for the monkeys.
evidence: Characterization of the task nature.

claim: The game being a foraging task may be the key to the successful training.
source: While the game is highly dynamic and complex, it is essentially a foraging task, which may be the key to the successful training.
evidence: Speculation about the reason for training success.

claim: The game has a clear objective, but an optimal solution is computationally difficult.
source: The game has a clear objective, but an optimal solution is computationally difficult.
evidence: Statement about the computational complexity of the task.

source: However, a set of intuitive strategies would allow players to achieve reasonable performance.

claim: The dynamic compositional strategy model is inspired by recent advances in the artificial intelligence field in developing AI algorithms that solve the game with a multiagent approach.
source: To find out whether the monkeys' behavior can be decomposed into a set of strategies, we fit their gameplay with a dynamic compositional strategy model, which is inspired by recent advances in the artificial intelligence field in developing AI algorithms that solve the game with a multiagent approach (Foderaro et al., 2017; Rohlfshagen et al., 2018; Sutton et al., 1999; Van Seijen et al., 2017).
evidence: Description of the model's conceptual basis with citations.

claim: The model consists of a set of simple strategies, each considering a specific aspect of the game to form decisions on how to move Pac-Man.
source: The model consists of a set of simple strategies, each considering a specific aspect of the game to form decisions on how to move Pac-Man.

claim: The monkeys were able to use the strategies as building blocks to form compound strategies to handle particular game situations.
source: In addition, the monkeys were able to use the strategies as building blocks to form compound strategies to handle particular game situations.
evidence: Summary of findings about compound strategy use.

claim: Animals are capable of managing a set of compositional strategies and employing hierarchical decision-making to solve a complex task.
source: Our results demonstrated that animals are capable of managing a set of compositional strategies and employing hierarchical decision-making to solve a complex task.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study.

source: Previous studies revealed that non-luminance-mediated changes in pupil diameter can be used as markers of arousal, surprise, value, and other factors during decision-making (Joshi and Gold, 2020).

claim: The pupil dilation change reflected the decision-making at the middle level of the hierarchical model.
source: At the middle level, decisions are made between these basis strategies, most likely with a heuristic for the monkeys to reduce the complexity of the decision-making. The pupil dilation change reflected the decision-making at this level.
evidence: Interpretation of pupil dilation findings in the context of the hierarchical model.

claim: The compound strategies are not simple impromptu strategy assemblies.
source: These compound strategies are not simple impromptu strategy assemblies. Instead, they may reflect more advanced planning.
evidence: Interpretation of the nature of compound strategies.

source: With this criterion, we extracted 493 (Monkey O) and 463 (Monkey P) planned attack plays, and 1970 (Monkey O) and 1295 (Monkey P) accidental consumption plays in our dataset.

source: With this criterion, we extracted 493 (Monkey O) and 463 (Monkey P) planned attack plays, and 1970 (Monkey O) and 1295 (Monkey P) accidental consumption plays in our dataset.
evidence: Quantitative description of behavior categorization.

source: With this criterion, we extracted 493 (Monkey O) and 463 (Monkey P) planned attack plays, and 1970 (Monkey O) and 1295 (Monkey P) accidental consumption plays in our dataset.

source: With this criterion, we extracted 493 (Monkey O) and 463 (Monkey P) planned attack plays, and 1970 (Monkey O) and 1295 (Monkey P) accidental consumption plays in our dataset.

claim: The decision of switching to the approach strategy was not an afterthought but planned well ahead.
source: The weight dynamics suggest that the decision of switching to the approach strategy was not an afterthought but planned well ahead.
evidence: Interpretation of strategy weight dynamics.

claim: The monkeys strung the energizer/local strategy with the approach strategy together into the compound strategy to eat an energizer and then hunt the ghosts.
source: The monkeys strung the energizer/local strategy with the approach strategy together into the compound strategy to eat an energizer and then hunt the ghosts.
evidence: Description of compound strategy formation.

claim: The death of Pac-Man resets the game and returns Pac-Man and the ghosts to their starting positions in the maze.
source: The death of Pac-Man resets the game and returns Pac-Man and the ghosts to their starting positions in the maze.
evidence: Description of game mechanics.

claim: It is advantageous to reset the game by committing suicide when local pellets are scarce, and the remaining pellets are far away.
source: As the only punishment in the monkey version of the game is a time-out, it is advantageous to reset the game by committing such suicide when local pellets are scarce, and the remaining pellets are far away.
evidence: Logical reasoning about optimal strategy in specific game contexts.

claim: In suicides, Pac-Man's death significantly reduced the distance to the closest pellets.
source: In suicides, Pac-Man's death significantly reduced this distance (Figure 6A, upper histogram, Figure 6—video 1, individual monkeys: Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: Quantitative analysis of the effect of suicide behavior.

claim: The suicides were a proactive decision.
source: Therefore, these suicides were a proactive decision.
evidence: Interpretation based on multiple lines of evidence.

claim: The death was anticipated in suicides.
source: Their pupil size decreased even before Pac-Man's death in suicides, which was significantly smaller than in failed evasions, suggesting that the death was anticipated (Figure 6D, p<0.01, two-sample t-test, individual monkeys: Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and H).
evidence: Interpretation of pupil dilation data.

claim: The compositional strategy model not only provides a good fit for the monkeys' behavior but also offers insights into the monkeys' gameplay.
source: Together, these two examples demonstrated how monkeys' advanced gameplay can be understood with concatenated basis strategies. The compositional strategy model not only provides a good fit for the monkeys' behavior but also offers insights into the monkeys' gameplay.
evidence: Summary statement about the utility of the model.

claim: The compound strategies demonstrate that the monkeys learned to actively change the game into desirable states that can be solved with planned strategies.
source: The compound strategies demonstrate that the monkeys learned to actively change the game into desirable states that can be solved with planned strategies.
evidence: Interpretation of compound strategy behavior.

claim: Such intelligent behavior cannot be explained with a passive foraging strategy.
source: Such intelligent behavior cannot be explained with a passive foraging strategy.
evidence: Conclusion about the nature of the observed behavior.

claim: Pursuing a deeper insight into the cognitive capability of the brain demands sophisticated behavior paradigms in which an ensemble of perception, attention, valuation, executive control, decision-making, motor planning, and other cognitive processes need to work together continuously across time.
source: Just as one cannot gain a full understanding of the visual system by studying it with bars and dots, pursuing a deeper insight into the cognitive capability of the brain demands sophisticated behavior paradigms in which an ensemble of perception, attention, valuation, executive control, decision-making, motor planning, and other cognitive processes need to work together continuously across time.
evidence: Argument for the need for complex behavioral paradigms.

claim: The behavior of monkeys during a complex game can be understood and described with a set of basis strategies that decompose the decision-making into different hierarchies.
source: Naturally, quantifying and modeling these behaviors in such paradigms is challenging, but here we demonstrated that the behavior of monkeys during a complex game can be understood and described with a set of basis strategies that decompose the decision-making into different hierarchies.
evidence: Summary of the main contribution of the study.

claim: The hierarchical model explains the monkeys' joystick movements well.
source: Our hierarchical model explains the monkeys' joystick movements well (Figure 2B).
evidence: Statement about model performance with figure reference.

claim: The strategies derived from the model can be verified with independent behavior measurements.
source: Importantly, the strategies derived from the model can be verified with independent behavior measurements.
evidence: Statement about the validation approach.

claim: The monkeys' fixation pattern reflected the features associated with the current strategy.
source: The monkeys' fixation pattern, a measure of their attention, reflected the features associated with the current strategy (Figure 3E).
evidence: Eye tracking analysis supporting the model.

claim: An increase in pupil dilation was found at the deduced strategy switches.
source: Moreover, an increase in pupil dilation (Figure 3F), which was not associated with any particular changes of game states, was found at the deduced strategy switches.
evidence: Pupil dilation analysis supporting the model.

claim: This is consistent with the prediction from the hierarchical model that there should be crucial decision-making of strategies around the strategy transitions.
source: This is consistent with the prediction from the hierarchical model that there should be crucial decision-making of strategies around the strategy transitions.
evidence: Interpretation linking pupil dilation findings to model predictions.

claim: Flat models are much more computationally costly than hierarchical models.
source: Although in theory a flat model may achieve equal or even greater performance than a hierarchical model, flat models are much more computationally costly.
evidence: Theoretical comparison of model types.

claim: When working memory has a limited capacity, hierarchical models can achieve a faster and more accurate performance.
source: Especially when working memory has a limited capacity, as in the case of the real brain, hierarchical models can achieve a faster and more accurate performance (Botvinick and Weinstein, 2014).
evidence: Statement about hierarchical model advantages with citation.

claim: Even for a complex flat model such as Deep Q-Network, the game performance is much worse than a hierarchical model.
source: Even for a complex flat model such as Deep Q-Network, which evaluates primitive actions directly with a deep learning network structure without any temporally extended higher-level decisions (Mnih et al., 2015), the game performance is much worse than a hierarchical model (Van Seijen et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with AI models with citations.

claim: The most successful AI player to date uses a multiagent solution, which is hierarchical in nature.
source: In fact, the most successful AI player to date uses a multiagent solution, which is hierarchical in nature (Van Seijen et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about AI approaches with citation.

claim: The monkeys also adopted a hierarchical solution for the Pac-Man game.
source: Our study shows that the monkeys also adopted a hierarchical solution for the Pac-Man game.
evidence: Main conclusion of the study.

claim: The particular set of basis strategies in the model is hand-crafted.
source: Although the particular set of basis strategies in the model is hand-crafted, we have good reasons to believe that they reflect the decision-making of the monkeys.
evidence: Acknowledgment of model design choice.

claim: The model fitting procedure is agnostic to how one should choose between the strategies.
source: Our model fitting procedure is agnostic to how one should choose between the strategies, yet the resulting strategies can be corroborated both from monkeys' route planning, eye movements, and pupil dilation patterns.
evidence: Description of the model fitting approach and validation.

claim: The correlation between the results of strategy fitting and the fixation patterns of the monkeys indicates that the animals learned to selectively attend to the features that were relevant for their current strategy while ignoring others to reduce the cognitive load for different states.
source: The correlation between the results of strategy fitting and the fixation patterns of the monkeys indicates that the animals learned to selectively attend to the features that were relevant for their current strategy while ignoring others to reduce the cognitive load for different states.
evidence: Interpretation of the relationship between model results and eye tracking data.

claim: Similar behaviors have also been observed in human studies.
source: Similar behaviors have also been observed in human studies (Leong et al., 2017; Wilson and Niv, 2011).
evidence: Comparison with human research with citations.

claim: The pupil dilation at the time of strategy transitions indicated the extra cognitive processing carried out in the brain to handle the strategy transitions.
source: In particular, the pupil dilation at the time of strategy transitions indicated the extra cognitive processing carried out in the brain to handle the strategy transitions.
evidence: Interpretation of pupil dilation findings.

claim: The model, without being specified so, revealed that a single strategy dominates monkeys' decision-making during most of the game.
source: Lastly, the model, without being specified so, revealed that a single strategy dominates monkeys' decision-making during most of the game.
evidence: Emergent finding from the model fitting.

claim: This is consistent with the idea that strategy-using is a method that the brain uses to simplify decision-making by ignoring irrelevant game aspects to solve complex tasks.
source: This is consistent with the idea that strategy-using is a method that the brain uses to simplify decision-making by ignoring irrelevant game aspects to solve complex tasks (Binz et al., 2022; Moreno-Bote et al., 2020).
evidence: Interpretation with citations to relevant literature.

claim: In some previous animal studies, strategies were equated to decision rules.
source: In some previous animal studies, strategies were equated to decision rules (Bunge and Wallis, 2007; Genovesio and Wise, 2007; Hoshi et al., 2000; Mante et al., 2013; Tsujimoto et al., 2011).
evidence: Literature review with citations.

claim: The rules in previous studies were typically mutually exclusive, and the appropriate rule was either specified with explicit sensory cues or the trial-block structure.
source: The rules were typically mutually exclusive, and the appropriate rule was either specified with explicit sensory cues or the trial-block structure.
evidence: Description of previous research approaches.

claim: The rules in previous studies can be boiled down to simple associations.
source: The rules in these studies can be boiled down to simple associations, even in cases when the association may be abstract (Genovesio and Wise, 2007).
evidence: Characterization of previous research with citation.

claim: In this study, strategies are defined as a heuristic that reduces a complex computation into a set of smaller and more manageable problems or computations.
source: In this study, however, we defined a set of strategies as a heuristic that reduces a complex computation into a set of smaller and more manageable problems or computations.
evidence: Definition of the concept of strategy used in the study.

claim: There were no explicit cues or trial-block structures to instruct animals on which strategies to choose.
source: There were no explicit cues or trial-block structures to instruct animals on which strategies to choose.
evidence: Description of the experimental design.

claim: The same prefrontal network, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, and polar cortex that are suggested to engage in rule use and rule switching, may also play important roles in strategy-based decision-making.
source: Nevertheless, the same prefrontal network, including the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, orbitofrontal cortex, and polar cortex that are suggested to engage in rule use and rule switching (Bunge and Wallis, 2007; Genovesio and Wise, 2007; Hoshi et al., 2000; Mante et al., 2013; Tsujimoto et al., 2011), may also play important roles in strategy-based decision-making, too.
